author: Freedom Editor
title: “Britain or Ireland? Neither nation, thanks”
content: Interview: Rave punk provocateurs Them’uns on anti-sectarianism and anti-militarism Them’uns are a rave punk duo from a rural town in north County Antrim (they won’t say which one). On 11 November (Armistice Day), they released a track titled ‘Amarum’, which is Latin for ‘bitter’ – inverting war poet Wilfred Owen’s famous ‘old lie’: Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori. But aside from the anti-militarist bangers, but what sort of ‘them’uns’ are Them’uns, exactly? And why is a punk band singing in Latin? We caught up with Jim from the duo to explain… Let’s start with the obvious question: why ‘Them’uns’? Well, there’s a cheeky nod to the old 1960s beat band ‘Them’ from Belfast – though we sound nothing like them, have zero sympathies with Van Morrison’s recent eejitry, and we’re emphatically NOT from Belfast. Then there’s the Norn Irn ‘identity’ bit. In this part of the world, them’uns are the others – we don’t take either side in the ‘two traditions’ carve up, so we’ll always be apart from the mainstream blocs seeking an Irish Union or British Nation (yes, you heard that last bit correctly). You might call us ‘neither-nors’, but not in the limp non-sectarian sense. We’re anti-sectarian anarchists. Is it the ‘anarchist’ provocation that makes you a punk band then, despite all the synthesisers and electronic drum malarkey? Provocation? Yeah, why not? When supposed counter-culturalists allow themselves to be sucked into the mire of nationalism – of any colour – they’re losing any critical edge they might have had. And, look, I know people are hopelessly wedded to their guitar bands, but synthesisers are by far a more democratic instrument. Synths and e-drums are punker than guitars, because anyone really can do it. How’s that for a provocation? And there’s a ton of distortion on everything, if that helps us retain some punk cred. I’m not the arbiter of punk credibility! Let’s get into the new track ‘Amarum’. I can see you’ve lifted some lines from the War poets like Siegfried Sassoon, Charles Hamilton Sorley, and of course Wilfred Owen. But aren’t you losing Owen’s irony by going directly with ‘Bitter and shameful’? (And since when do punk bands sing in Latin, by the way?) The internet killed irony dead! It’s not that people are dumbed-down or too stupid to get it; the online ecosystem is just so full of people arguing in bad faith. They strip away context and nuance, and irony relies entirely on context and nuance, so it’s just become useless nowadays. We have to say it plainly: ‘it’s bitter and shameful to die for your country’. The shame is not on those who die, but on the countries that send them off to be butchered. The bitterness is felt by those staring death in its miserable eye, and by everyone they leave behind. That’s exactly what Owen and the rest of them were saying in the First World War, right? It’s the same meaning with ‘Amarum’, it’s just as anti-militarist, but there’s no room for subtle poesy these days. Amarum by Them’uns This isn’t a pacifist thing, and it’s not a ‘both sides-ism’ thing. But we need to show some anti-militarist spine in the face of aggressively asserted nationalisms – people get swept up in the fervour, alienate ‘other’ humans, and then deadly violence can be excused and even celebrated. You can attach whatever decorous ‘nobility’ you want to that, but we need to ask ourselves: who benefits from our martyrdom? Did you say you were going to send this to Freedom? Maybe we need to do a side mission on Kropotkin? Well, there are a lot of resonances with the build up to the Great War nowadays. But maybe we’ll let him off the hook since he’s been dead for 105 years. Do you think Prince Piotr would have been a rave punk fan? No, Goldman’s the rave punk, for sure. Kropotkin would be into post-hardcore – earnest but with barely concealed mainstream pretensions. Bakunin’s obviously a crusty. Proudhon fronts up a gruff pop punk/orgcore band. Landauer’s an emo. I could go on … So is it true that you’ve got a PhD in Political Philosophy, then? Good to see it being put to good use there Jim. No comment! Speaking of unlikely punk languages, we did do a song in Ulster Scots too. That’s probably more provocative than anything else we’ve said or done, which tells you a lot about the state of ‘cultural warfare’ here in the north of Ireland. Punk Rave EP by Them’uns I was going to ask about that. I’m reminded of another Northern Irish ravey duo, Fun Protestants. You’re both effectively playing up this ‘identity’ angle – is it basically a proddy version of Kneecap? Now you’re the one trying to be provocative! We’ve played with Fun Protestants once before – really dead on people, and I love the music, their album’s great. I can see why you’d point to a similarity, and I’d take it as a compliment. I think what Fun Protestants do is really important, skewering their own cultural background, and maybe in the process pointing to something liberatory and radical that runs through Protestantism in the north of Ireland. But again, I would worry that the ironic critique made by Fun Protestants just gets turned into blatant sectarianism by other people who won’t admit that there’s a progressive element there, or that their own ‘side’ is guilty of similarly regressive small-mindedness. Them’uns takes aim at both sides simultaneously – we have to, because as soon as you pick a side, the game’s over. Like, that’s the opposite of ‘both-sides-ism’, isn’t it? It’s neither-side-ism. You’re reminding me of ‘80s anarcho-punk bands like Toxic Waste with that: ‘Choose and be damned’! Exactly! There were ‘alternative’ bands flirting with nationalism/unionism back then too, of course – That Petrol Emotion and Ruefrex and some other bands spinning off from the punk scene. If it was tragic then, I suppose it must be farcical now. I’ve got a better one for you: ‘If you can’t laugh at yourself, I’ll be happy to do it for you’ – that’s Groucho. Point taken! But I did notice a review in the luminary punk zine MaximumRockNRoll that described Them’uns as ‘British’ – where did that come from? A lazy reviewer! We sent MRR a cassette tape (This is Rave Punk, 2023), but they only ever listened to the Bandcamp page – which had the location set to ‘Antrim, UK’, so the reviewer just decided UK meant Britain, and that therefore we were British. Of course we’re not. We’re from the island of Ireland (but if Ed Sheeran’s ‘Irish’, then we’re not that either, and we’re certainly not going about wearing a tricolour balaclava). But why would you expect a self-satisfied US zine reviewer to understand that sort of geopolitical complexity? He didn’t even listen to the actual tape! There were different versions of the songs on the Bandcamp page – and one song wasn’t on there at all, it was tape-only, so it was obvious that he hadn’t bothered. He didn’t give us a particularly favourable review either (described us as ‘textbook anti-authoritarian’) which might explain why I’m so grumpy about it. Do better next time, Nick Odorizzi! Yes, I feel like you’re bearing a bit of a grudge there, Jim. I thought the first two tapes were a lot of fun, if that’s any consolation. But the new song has a different feel to it. Is that fair to say? Is ‘fun’ a back-handed compliment, Ian? But yeah, that’s fair. We had a line-up change earlier this year. Amy’s come in and plays some lead synth, which we didn’t have before. The e-drum set up has been stripped back to just two pads. And we recorded this one ourselves, so maybe it’s a bit more raw but more musically expansive? We pretend to make a punk virtue out of capturing all the sounds live, rather than relying on production tricks – but honestly we were just worried that we’d screw it up because we’re not that clever at using Digital Audio Workstation software. We spent time getting the right sounds to come out of the synths and amps and microphones, and then just mixed that – there’s not even any equalisation on it! I’m willing to award some bonus punk points for that. So, give us the plug then – how can people hear it? ‘Amarum’ is coming out as a digital thing with Do It With Others Records, and all their proceeds go directly to anarchist causes. DIWO do everything as ‘pay what you want’ – kudos to Marko! Two more tracks from that recording session are coming out as a DIY 7” vinyl release on 11th December, titled ‘Ballymetropolis’/‘Mouth Ulster’ – we’re playing a gig locally in Coleraine to launch that one. There’s a streamable version on Bandcamp, and you can pre-order the physical record there too. author: Freedom Editor
title: A day of general strike in Spain
content:
A chronicle of pre-dawn picket lines, massive demonstrations, persistent rain, and sharply differing figures on participation

The strike began before dawn. By midnight, the first picket lines were already being organized. In Valencia, the CGT union had called for pickets at the Mercavalència wholesale market starting at 2:00 a.m., and at the EMT (municipal transport) depots in San Isidro from 5:00 a.m. Subsequently, access routes into the city—including the V-21 highway and the Ronda Nord—were blocked. The coverage in Valencia tracked the movement from the wholesale markets to the municipal transport network.

In Catalonia, actions were concentrated from the early hours at the Mercabarna wholesale market, various workplaces, and along roadways. According to updates published throughout the morning, more than thirty locations across the road network were affected by blockades. In Madrid, “informational” picket lines gathered at the EMT transport depots in Fuencarral and Carabanchel; the CCOO and UGT unions reported police charges and the use of pepper spray against participants.

At the Mercamadrid wholesale market, unions also reported police intervention. Reports concerning the Madrid transport depots include statements from the organisations involved. Tension spread to Málaga, where reports emerged of police charges near the EMT (municipal transport company) depots, and to Zamora, where early reports indicated two arrests and four people requiring emergency medical attention following an incident involving a transport picket line. In the Basque Country, the Ertzaintza (Basque police) reported thirteen arrests as of mid-morning, eight of which took place in Portugalete. These were preliminary tallies from different regions and points in time.

Initial reports from labour unions indicated high participation in certain industrial sectors. CCOO and UGT estimated that 90% of workers in the automotive and port sectors, and 85% in the meat-processing industry, participated during the early shifts. The CGT also reported high levels of work stoppages and picket activity. These estimates come from the organisations themselves, refer to specific sectors and shifts, and do not, on their own, confirm the overall percentage of workers on strike. The initial industrial report provides further detail on its source.

In the Valencian Community, the figures varied significantly. UGT-PV reported over 70% participation in industrial firms with union representation, while the employers’ association, CEV, estimated a 2.57% participation rate across the region’s entire economic sector during the early hours. Later, CCOO and UGT reported an average participation rate of 60% in the region. These figures are not directly comparable, as they differ in scope, the population observed, and the timeframes considered. Examining both sets of figures helps to explain these discrepancies.

The strike also affected public media. Canal Sur Televisión interrupted its regular programming around 8:20 a.m. while the show Despierta Andalucía was airing. In Valencia, nearly fifty students staged a sit-in at the Faculty of Geography and History at the University of Valencia in support of the strike. Picket groups focused on commercial areas moved through the streets and neighbourhoods of various cities. In the Vila de Gràcia neighbourhood, the mobilisation coincided with the postponement of an eviction.

The struggle for housing did not emerge as an issue separate from working conditions. Tenants’ unions, labour unions, and neighbourhood assemblies brought demands against high rents to the picket lines, alongside the defence of wages, public services, and labour rights. In Bilbao, groups converged in front of the Arriaga Theatre before heading toward the Basque Government headquarters. In Pamplona (Iruñea), a protest in front of CaixaBank ended with one arrest, according to reports on the day’s events. In Barcelona, ​​a main picket line moved through the commercial district; in Madrid, there were blockades on the Gran Vía and the Carrera de San Jerónimo.

By the afternoon, the strike had reached the major avenues.

Barcelona saw one of the largest marches. Groups arriving from various neighborhoods converged at the Jardinets and the Passeig de Gràcia. The Tenants’ Union (Sindicat de Llogateres) estimated the turnout at 400,000 people, while the local police (Guardia Urbana) provided an estimate of 55,000. These figures come from different sources, with no independent assessment to resolve the discrepancy. After the march concluded, La Directa and El Salto reported that the Mossos (Catalan police) had carried out charges in the city centre.

In Valencia, a unified demonstration took place in the rain. The march moved along Calle Colón and reached the Plaza del Ayuntamiento, with participation from labour unions and housing advocacy groups. El Salto reported tens of thousands of participants, while other media outlets described thousands of attendees and a historic demonstration. The live coverage by Sindicalismo.org could not verify an exact figure provided by the organisers; therefore, that description is not translated here into a specific number. Levante-EMV and Europa Press published accounts of the march.

In Zaragoza, the National Police estimated 20,000 protesters, while the organisers claimed 60,000. In Lleida, the Guardia Urbana (local police) estimated 4,500 attendees, compared to 14,000 according to the unions. In Granada, El Salto reported two separate marches, estimating at least 8,000 people in each. Girona and Manresa also saw large-scale demonstrations, according to the organising groups. In Madrid, the march from Atocha toward Plaza de España proceeded through the rain, with housing issues serving as one of its central demands.

Severe weather impacted the day’s events in Andalusia. CCOO and UGT canceled their afternoon demonstrations in Cádiz, Huelva, Córdoba, and Seville as conditions worsened. However, a separate mobilisation took place in Seville, organised by housing groups and organisations such as the CGT, CNT, and USTEA. The cancellation of one event did not mean that all protests in the city were called off.

Reports of police charges and the identification of individuals emerged alongside the strike, beginning with the very first picket lines. In Granada, the Andalusian Association for Human Rights (Asociación Pro Derechos Humanos de Andalucía) called for an investigation into police interventions near the Metro and the Alhambra, reporting a rib injury and difficulties in identifying the officers involved. In Madrid, El Salto reported the use of pepper spray and rubber bullets during an intervention that took place after the demonstration had concluded, in the area of ​​Plaza de España. In Tarragona, Alerta Solidària reported that individuals were injured by foam projectiles during a protest near the Palau de Congressos. These are reported incidents and allegations attributed to specific sources, not judicial findings.

The tally of arrests published by Sindicalismo.org recorded 52 detainees and 919 incidents as of 5:00 PM, based on data available at that time from the Ministry of the Interior and regional police forces: 38 arrests by the National Police and Civil Guard, 13 reported by the Ertzaintza, and one by the Mossos. This figure superseded previous counts of 40 and 42 arrests; these numbers should not be added together.

The figures shifted later that evening: at 9:45 PM, the Mossos reported 18 arrests in the centre of Barcelona—a local figure that emerged after the 5:00 PM national tally. This cannot simply be added to the 52 without first verifying potential overlaps or the timing of the events. Trade unions and anti-repression organisations demanded explanations and defended the right to strike, while police forces justified their interventions by citing incidents they attributed to protesters. A final, definitive figure for the entire day was not available from the sources consulted for this report.

author: Freedom Editor
title: Dignity walks in the heart
content:
Mexico’s search collectives make alliances with Zapatista army to confront the systematic violence of enforced disappearances and femicides

It is dawn again and 12-year-old Ariana is getting ready to leave her home with her grandmother. Together they walk in the mountains of Chiapas to a nearby ranch to care for their family animals. After that? We cannot say, as they both stepped out of this world and disappeared. We only know for sure that they were never seen alive again.

The family and neighbours began the search until two days later, the body of 55-year-old Miriam Cruz Alpuche was discovered on the bank of a local stream. She was wrapped in black bin bags and community rescue units discovered multiple signs of violence. By the end of the week, Ariana Scarlet Velázquez Cruz was found close by.

“The demand for truth and justice for disappearances,” said Captain Marcos of the EZLN (Zapatista Army of National Liberation) “enforced disappearances and disappearances by individuals – must be assumed a national responsibility.” Marcos was speaking in San Cristóbal de las Casas (Jovel) in Chiapas after meeting with “mother seekers” in el caracol Jacinto Canel.

In the Zapatista territories, EZLN and colectivos de búsqueda (search collectives) have pledged to form alliances in confronting the Mexican government for it’s role in facilitating disappearances, murders, gender-based violence and wars. They will meet in Ajusco in December, an area that is a high risk for disappearances, as well as a delegation to Mexico City to both expose and find community-based resistance to this crime against humanity.

With more than 130,000 people missing in Mexico, decades of activism and legal battles against systematic violence and enforced disappearances, the United Nations has finally got involved in offering the state of Mexico assistance. Predictably as the families of the disappeared arrived to give their own testimony, the Mexican government denied this pain with their own historical fiction.

In Chiapas there have been 30 documented cases of femicide and 440 across Mexico in the first half of 2026. These numbers are reflections of the activities of local groups, not the true scale of the problem. Government corruption has hidden the mass killings of women and children, as well as a clear complicity in the enforced disappearances of it’s own citizens. If the body is never recovered, it cannot be known how the person died.

Investigations into femicides in Mexico are impacted by a loss of evidence, an inadequate investigation or when the gender perspective is not applied correctly. Families of the missing are re-victimised by the process of seeking justice while authorities fail to examine crime scenes, secure evidence or carry out acid phosphatase tests. All of this impacts the possibility of justice for the affected and their families.

Femicidal violence “leaves indelible consequences, deep traumas and an irreparable void in their families… in their communities and in the entire social fabric of the state,” said the Observatorio Ciudadano Nacional del Feminicidio (National Citizen Observatory of Femicide) following the murder of Miriam and Ariana. They demand an immediate gender – child perspective investigation.

The inaction of the authorities when a woman or child has gone missing is deadly, with some regional police asking families to wait 72 hours before reporting a missing person. This would have been too late for Miriam, as it would likely be for 12-year-old Ariana. The logic should be to investigate when a person is noticed missing.

In the absence of executing justice, various instruments of the law such as the Attorney General’s Office (FGE) work as a mechanism to prevent the opening of investigations, with “omission… a lack of commitment and responsibility,” observed Guadalupe Isabel Mondoza Pérez, who has been looking for her husband Alfonso since July 30, 2024 after he disappeared in Yajalón.

Authorities limit complaints by creating an administrative hole called “registros de attención” (care records) as a way of killing formal investigations. With legal advice from Colectiva Cereza (Cherry Collective), families can see what missing persons reports have been shelved in care records and which are open investigations.

If the aim is to tear the social fabric of our shared relations – it would make sense to weave these communities with shared struggles and resources to resist the stranglehold of the law as systematic violence. It is a rebellion to demand social responsibility from top to bottom and reach out to those who seek justice for their loved ones; dead, alive or caught in between.

What unites all activists in the various regional search collectives is a rejection of the government’s narrative of the decline of disappearances and token offerings of dedicated government departments that seemingly do nothing to combat the 40 disappearances a day or provide effective prevention strategies to address the problem.

María Tequi, founder of the Guerreras Buscadoras de Guaymas collective denounced the government’s strategy of making the disappearances in Chiapas invisible by claiming that the reasons why young men are missing are because they migrated to get a job. This narrative is powerful on both southern and northern borders, claiming that people are missing because they left “to work out of necessity.”

“They keep disappearing, they keep killing us. The missing are not absent” María says, “our disappeared are missing because the were taken away, they are not absent of their own free will.” María continues to search for her son Fernando who disappeared in August 2015.

Speaking to the United Nations, Cristina Bautista explained how she will continue to demand justice for her son Benjamin, who on the night of the September 26, 2014 was disappeared with 43 other students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers’ College by the local, state and federal police, in collusion with criminal organisations and the military.

“If we, as fathers and mothers of the 43 students of Ayotzinapa do not shut up, it is so that it does not continue to happen to the other parents, to the other students, that they do not continue to disappear because it is a very great suffering.” By sunrise on September 27; six people were dead, forty wounded and 43 missing. Most of these enforced disappearances have never been found.

The government investigated itself and the Attorney General’s Office came up with it’s own narrative of events calling it “historical truth.” Yet the findings of Forensic Architecture and local civil society collectives discovered a constructed, fraudulent and inconsistent narrative. This fiction protects the impunity of the Mexican state, as it’s governments play both policeman and murderer in a play where half of the cast are missing from the stage.

Almost three decades ago we remember the 1997 massacre in Acteal, where 100 paramilitary soldiers entered a church and murdered 45 people who had taken refuge there. The victims were mostly woman and children and all were members of Las Abejas (The Bees), a libertarian pacifist group who were politically sympathetic to the EZLN. The local police and military refused to intervene as the massacre went on for hours.

The Mexican government denied involvement but leaked plans for a counter-insurgency in Chiapas disproved this assertion, as does the fact that the old paramilitary structures of the 1990 remain intact, with some of the perpetrators of the massacres continuing raids. When tyranny is law, horizontal solidarity with groups and resources is our only way to challenge this form of systematic violence.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum believes the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances (CED) is over-reaching it’s mandate because there is ‘progress’ in the search for missing persons and the government is in ‘dialogue’ with the families of the missing. Enforced disappearance is a crime against humanity, even if committed by individuals under consent of state actors.

“We are concerned,” said Elizabeth Uruchurtu at the UN, “that in order to please it’s political allies, an image of a state that imparts justice is presented when it does not correspond to the reality we live. Enforced disappearance not only disappears people, it also tries to disappear truth, destroy evidence, sow fear and guarantee impunity.”

Daniela González has been looking for her 16-year-old son Axel since June 23, 2022 when he disappeared. Like many, Daniela had to organise to get justice for her son and is now a member of the search collective Una Luz en el Camino.

“The truth is that we have long sought this meeting, this dialogue with the Zapatista army,” Daniela said. “Fortunately today it is achieved and not only is dialogue but it is to be able to weave community, be able to knit and embrace to continue looking for our loved ones.”

“We recognize their struggle,” families of the missing wrote before the meeting, “and the exercise of autonomy and resistance to power, as well as the search for ways to a dignified life.”

author: Freedom Editor
title: A regressive love-letter to traditional journalism
content:
Film review: The Social Reckoning is both deeply attached to the liberal United States and terrified of what it has become

When history is written, how will the last 30 years be remembered? If The Social Reckoning is anything to go by, it will be as a slow slide into a paranoid dystopia. This film presents the most depressing view of the contemporary United States that I have seen to date, and that it does so from the heart of the Hollywood mainstream only makes this more striking. This is a shamelessly conservative romance that idealises middle-class, liberal and sexist American values in contrast to today’s proto-fascist, hyper-capitalist hellscape.

Frances Haugan, whose ethical compass is the film’s North star, is in a codependent relationship with her company. She loves Facebook, but when she stumbles on evidence of its corrupting influence, she is unable to raise the problem internally, and expects to be caught and punished for blowing the whistle. Like a late-period Stasi spy, she quickly comes to distrust her superiors, her society, and the other side, while remaining attached to a myth of instant, universal connection.

In the USSR, that myth was of communism as an approaching, abundant and benevolent equality. Here, Frances’s utopia is a world without “human friction”, where everyone communicates and everyone gets along. The spanner in the works is the profit motive. Its representative, Mark Zuckerberg, seems cut straight out of an Ayn Rand novel: buff, dominant and visionary, anti-social and intensely self-interested.

The reality of Facebook was already far more compromised than this film wishes to suggest – from its origins as a mysogynistic comparison app, to its key role in the Cambridge Analytica scandal in 2018 – but this would complicate the film’s regressive love-letter to traditional journalism. It is Jeff Horwitz’ role to discover the truth we all already know, that massive corporations with a free at the point-of-use model cannot be trusted.

This is a film which is both deeply attached to the liberal United States and terrified of what it has become. This is an America in which corporations are “post-government”, in which coup attempts are whipped up by false information, and in which a “free speech absolutist” cynically stokes conflict to sell more ads. This is an America that is twilit both literally and metaphorically, and where our hard-working, middle-class heroes are reduced to a whisper. This is an America that is a long way from a happy ending.

The film is also a kind of heteronormative romance. Haugan, presented as single, isolated, and girlish, is slowly seduced into disclosing the truth by Horwitz’ older, experienced journalist. He is respectful, modest, and a listener, the opposite of the Silicon Valley bros she is surrounded by. As she becomes a source, she is increasingly – and unnecessarily – sexualised. In the final scene she appears without the ankle and wrist warmers she wears to help with the symptoms of coeliac disease – she doesn’t want to look like a “freak” – and he holds her by the wrists.

The degree of conservatism here is a marker of just how far to the right the mainstream has shifted. “I work at the Wall Street Journal, so my cred as a free-market capitalist is solid” intones one, well-meaning-but-tough stereotype of the female boss, “and even I think this needs government intervention.” This is not the place to look for the sort of revolutionary propaganda of Sorry to Bother You, or even the deeply compromised Hollywood radicalism of One Battle After Another. This is movie shot through with conservative nostalgia for the pre-internet status quo.

And yet, as shoe-leather journalism disappears further and further into the rear view and AI gobbles up the last of the intellectual jobs already taken by neoliberalism and social media, there is something worth holding onto in this tradition. As me and my partner were walking home, we watched an unconfirmed but deeply concerning story from Facebook about a young girl being followed by racialised men was reposted onto our local group chat, without context, by several well-meaning activists in the area. In these moments the value of trustworthy people investigating the truth behind rumours, distortion, and sensationalism is immediately clear.

From behind a screen, these narratives can stoke any number of anxieties, from fears the far-right will whip up racial violence from false accusations, to concern that gender-based abuse is being perpetrated without consequence. We need to support people to dig into the facts, as well as the perspectives and interests of all those involved, if we are to build a society we can feel safe within.

This film presents a conflict between two poles. On one side is an emerging alliance between libertarian monopoly capital and the fascist right. On the other is an idealised coalition of middle-class professionals, competitive businesses, and small-c conservatives. As anarchists, we have to construct an anti-statist egalitarian movement that can challenge both these alternatives. To do so, we must learn how to trust each other, organise, and represent a genuinely progressive future.

author: Freedom Editor
title: Spycops: It only gets worse
content:
This year the Undercover Policing Inquiry was a one-stop horror shop of abuse stories

In 2026 the Undercover Policing Inquiry was a one-stop horror shop of stories perfectly demonstrating how the police, by its very nature, tends to abuses of power. Some were well-known, such as the targeting of the families of murdered teenagers and justice campaigns for people of colour. Others emerged during live evidence.

“Tranche 3” of the Inquiry covered the Special Demonstration Squad, the Metropolitan Police Special Branch unit which carried out most of the undercover work. The period was from 1992 to the end of 2007, when the SDS was shut down – for refusing to modernise. Live testimony came from the undercovers and managers, and their victims.

We continued to learn details of how many women were deceived into sexual relations. Among the most shocking accounts was that of ‘Maya’, who was targeted by the undercover Rob Hastings. The painful details of how the grief he gave her was drawn out wrecked everyone listening. Hastings sickeningly maintained he was the victim.

We also heard about HN14 Jim Boyling’s (pictured) central role in the June 18 Carnival Against Capitalism, and HN3 Jason Bishop’s around Mayday and the DSEi anti-arms trade protests.

There was smearing of activists to justify and extend deployments. Animal rights campaigner ‘L3’ went on a holiday to France with HN16 James Thomson, unaware that Thomson had cooked up an imaginary plot where he was buying a gun to avenge a friend injured by a hunter.

Anti-fascist activist ‘Kurt’ was targeted for arrest simply because he had seen HN15 Mark Jenner with his real wife – while Jenner, as ‘Mark Cassidy’, was deceiving ‘Alison’ into a five-year relationship and living in her house. HN104 Carlo Soracchi tried to encourage Socialist Party members to firebomb a charity shop.

Campaigners of colour were particularly maligned. Atif Choudhary, a ISM activist, was clearly racially profiled to boost the SDS’s standing, being wrongfully but deliberately linked with the Mike’s Place suicide bombers. A drunken conversation in a pub, where a white Globalise Resistance activist suggested wearing a fake suicide vest at an Ariel Sharon demonstration, was converted into a planned terror attack by a separate person of colour, ‘MT’, and only prevented by the courageous HN116 ‘Simon Wellings’ who talked him down. This fantasy was repeated in documents as a great success of the SDS.

Corruption abounded, and fraudulent documents were submitted to claim expenses. Donna McLean was astounded to be presented with a rent book in her name for when Sorracchi was living with her, claiming for twice the actual rent and forging her signature. Sorracchi and multiple managers all pointed the finger at each other but nobody had a proper explanation.

Likewise there was no explanation for numerous foreign trips which seemed to be junkets for all concerned. A stand-out was the protection of undercover HN5 John Dines from discovery by Helen Steel, who he had deceived into a relationship, which cost upwards of £3 million.

The SDS acted like a criminal gang, with its own culture and code of silence. Yet despite the Metropolitan Police opening the Tranche with a litany of apologies, SDS officers giving evidence were for the most part unable to see what they’d done wrong. Their constant lies and pretending not to remember were painful to watch. They were unable to accept that their precious Special Branch was fundamentally and institutionally anti-democratic.

The main impression one is left with is how badly-managed this “jewel in the crown” of Special Branch was. It was a defence of incompetence.

Only two outside officers were harsh in their criticism of the SDS, including Jon Boutcher, Chief Constable of Northern Ireland and the only serving officer to give evidence. Boucher stated the SDS had been out of control and the targeting of campaigners should never have happened.

The Inquiry still has to hear evidence from the other spycop unit, the National Public Order Intelligence Unit, which employed the likes of Mark Kennedy.

The Inquiry is in its 14th year, costing more than £130 million and another two years minimum are in the works. The delays are mostly, it has to be said, from excessive police secrecy. This summer, the Home Office announced a “consultation” on the future of the UCPI. With the current chair, Sir John Mitting, due to retire, nobody has been found to replace him.

This has raised fears of a cover-up, aimed at limiting the next stages or neutering the Inquiry in other ways. It is the MPS which has sat on much of the material which, had the victims received it sooner, would have shortened the Inquiry.

This article was first published in the Autumn/Winter issue of Freedom anarchist journal

author: Freedom Editor
title: The Whistles of Minneapolis
content:
How blowing a whistle to stop ICE raids opens up a challenge to the techno-fascists

The tools of state authoritarianism are changing fast. Swarms of drones levelling Gaza and mapping European airports; “flock” street cameras and cyber surveillance webs cataloguing everyone that moves through the major cities or uses a cell phone; state-directed bot armies using deep fake video and memes to alter people’s interior psyches.

A large part of the USA’s economic growth over the last few years has been the ever-larger digital surveillance and weapons industries, with Palantir and Amazon Web Services allowing governments to create vast databases of citizens’ lives, with ominous results. Digital and AI technologies have well-begun acting as accelerants of the domination and exhaustion of workers and the Earth’s ecologies. Commentators and scholars increasingly warn of geopolitical parallels with the twentieth century’s most wicked son, fascism.

Only this time the fash are equipped with expansive digital technologies of war, policing, surveillance, and propaganda.

But anti-fascist movements have begun to adapt, inventing organic technologies as new forms of counter-power. For example, when Trump sent Immigration Control and Enforcement (ICE), newly formed as a MAGA federal militia, to Minnesota to abduct, detain, and deport people of colour, organisers responded by mass 3-D printing a simple but effective technology: whistles. In Minneapolis, a longstanding hub of leftist organising, protesters wear these whistles as they take to the streets to disrupt ICE operations.

For more than a year, these same organisers and protestors have watched ICE agents on their city raids. Using encrypted cell phones to communicate to each other in Signal loops, they try to warn neighbours before the agents arrive. Thousands monitor the Signal loops for word of a raid, waiting for the moment to run out of their homes, blowing their anti-ICE whistles, so that all within earshot can try to flee the raids if they feel at risk. They are joined as community self-defence councils and more underground crews, with memberships in the tens of thousands. With some undocumented families hesitant to even leave their homes for fear of being disappeared by a federal sweep at the bus stops and outside of schools, mutual aid networks organise transportation networks to help their neighbours arrive at their workplaces and schools undetected.

The community councils have innovated on the road blockade to create what they call “filter blockades” across their neighbourhood streets, designed to allow neighbours to pass freely but prevent the passage of federal agents. Community defence crews counter-surveil federal authorities, setting up outside ICE’s headquarters at the Fort Snelling, a federal compound at the confluence of the Mississippi and Minnesota rivers that flow down through the North Woods and Western prairies. One hundred and fifty years ago, the United States Army forcibly marched thousands of Dakota Peoples into a concentration camp at the fort. Hundreds of Dakota prisoners died their first winter there, murdered, frozen to death, and starved. Now, federal forces carry out new forms of domination from the fort, part of what the federal government claims as their “unorganised territory” – lands never incorporated into any state or Native American government and thus under the direct control of the presidency through the Department of the Interior.

In Minneapolis’ Whittier neighbourhood, dissenters briefly raised an autonomous zone blockade at the site of the ICE murder of Alex Pretti, a nurse turned community defender. This is the same patch of concrete that, during the George Floyd uprisings, nurtured an epicenter of intense Black Lives Matter anti-police organising. From May 2020 until more than a year later, liberationists controlled a block of the neighbourhood as a police-free zone. Along the edge of Fort Snelling, an infrastructure that was and remains, as Nick Estes has called it, an infrastructure of U.S. power to genocide Indigenous people and Dakota people, organisers with First Nations United have started a Land Back protest and prayer camp on the land that was taken from their families more than a century ago. For these liberationists, only re-territorialising the land as Indigenous Land can end the cycles of history of white nationalist federal state detention and murder that have been perpetrated on the site.

These abolitionist tactics of not letting federal agents do their work uphold and make possible liberation struggles of many kinds. As it is practiced in the streets, self-defence against ICE becomes a logic against white nationalism because ICE targets people of colour, whom they construct to be the “illegals” of the global diaspora (no one is illegal). The uprisings also express logics of opposition to capitalism, because multinational capital seeks to restrict people’s freedoms of movement and mobilisation, not least across nation-state borders, to exploit the unevenness of global labour markets created by colonialism, imperialism, and unequal exchange. As the Trump administration labels those participating “antifa”, and formally declares them members of a domestic terrorist organisation, these people become revolutionaries in the eyes of the increasingly fascist state, willing or not.

Blowing a whistle to stop ICE raids opens up a challenge to the techno-fascists. So do the very low-tech efforts to help transport and harbour people targeted by the USA federal government for deportation. Still more organic technologies like these are needed to mount a serious rejection of the fash and the truly enormous amounts of energy the digital technologies of militarism and the consumer economy now demand. AI data centres will within the decade consume as much electricity as the nation of India. They will also consume vast amounts of freshwater. All this comes in an already destabilised climate with shrinking freshwater supplies worldwide. Day Zero, the moment when a major city runs out of fresh water, is already nearly here in Mexico City, Chennai, and Tehran. Los Angeles planners are working hard to continue expanding their ever-declining water sources, building new infrastructure to draw down water from ever more distant watersheds.

Fash power is partly techno-power, raising the need for struggles to create new organic technologies to uphold life free from domination and with a collective equality between human communities and broader communities of living beings. But any ecological politics that aims to respect human life, decarbonise and detoxify economies, and stop biological extinctions, must do so by countering far-right and capitalist structures. To “melt” ICE and stop the polar ice-caps from melting are but two components of the same struggle: to degrow the planetary economy so that it will not dominate planetary life.

This article was first published in Catalan

author: Freedom Editor
title: East London is anti-fascist
content:
Join us in Altab Ali Park on Saturday midday for a collective display of solidarity against the far right

On Saturday 31 October, neo-nazi thugs decided the best thing they could do with their day was take a trip to Freedom Bookshop in Whitechapel, and threaten and attack the volunteers and visitors to the shop.

The 15 or so masked up men filmed themselves spouting nonsense about “degenerate books” and making Hitler salutes. The volunteer locked the shop, a passerby confronted them and half the group fled. The man defended himself and was punched once before the rest of the group made their escape down Aldgate East tube.

Since then our heart has been warmed by the many expressions of solidarity.

As our friends from Plan C wrote, Freedom was attacked because it represents a history of anti-fascist resistance in East London.

Whilst this has happened to Freedom now, this concerns all of us. Let this be the catalyst to rally together.

Against fascist intimidation it is especially important to prioritise coming together, strengthening our existing networks, and organising for the sake of our community.

Join us in Altab Ali Park on Saturday midday for a collective display of solidarity against the far right.

author: Freedom Editor
title: Social reheating in Italy: Reflections on Friday’s mass strike
content:
The day was a breath of fresh air, with large turnouts opposing both war and the rising cost of living

30 October was a remarkable day. Not for many years has a strike called solely by grassroots trade unions achieved such success on a national level, with dozens upon dozens of local demonstrations filling streets and public squares. Various accounts highlight several common features: intergenerational participation, a significant role played by students, and a broad turnout of workers—all of which point to the clear success of the strike, even as the specific participation figures await further analysis.

Most striking, however, was the large number of young people—many of them very young, and some even minors—whom the government seeks to chain to school desks or factory benches, or else cast directly into juvenile detention centres. The first, clear outcome of 30 October was the overturning of fear. These major demonstrations reclaimed the public space—in squares, schools, universities, and workplaces. Repression was certainly present, with police charges in Rome, Turin, Vicenza, and Venice, alongside mass identity checks and pre-emptive detentions in many other cities.

author: Fenton
title: Serbian anarchists: Student List “perfectly in line” with neoliberalism
content:
Interview: Klasna Solidarnost members explain how popular assemblies were abused to install yet another pro-EU capitalist government

On 25 October, the “Student List” won a projected 140 of 250 seats in the Serbian parliament, defeating the ruling party that has been in power for 14 years. The electoral victory comes on the back of a student movement that began on 1 of November 2024, when a newly renovated canopy fell at the railway station in Novi Sad and killed sixteen people. Since then, people in Serbia have organised mass protests and assemblies.

We reached out to Klasna Solidarnost (Class Solirarity), founded in Belgrade in 2016, which grew out of an anarcho-syndicalist movement. Its members continue to participate in student occupations while critiquing electoral strategies. They are also active in antifascism, solidarity with Palestine, antimilitarism, support for workers, and the “Solidarna kuhinja” free kitchen, as well as political analysis and publications.

The mainstream media has presented the student movement as “decentralised” and highlighted the appointing of non-politicians to parliament; is this an accurate reflection of the movement now?

author: Freedom Editor
title: Why aren’t UK students revolting?
content:
We must see schools and universities as politically relevant, and build a shared sense of struggle with teachers and workers

Have you heard the news? British students have successfully begun forming a new government, with candidates chosen from their own movement after years of continuous uprising against corruption, forcing the 14-year oligarchy out!

Wait. That seems relatively uncharacteristic for British students? Oh yeah, of course—it wasn’t us. It was actually the Serbians, who forced now ex-president Aleksandar Vučić to announce a snap election for 25 October, which lost him 25 seats and his job.

Across Italy, Spain, Serbia, Portugal, Albania and France, protests against bad schooling, poor public services and the rising cost of living have been led by students. These deteriorating conditions are often linked to neo-liberalism: an economic and political adaptation of capitalism that prioritises the looting of public institutions and wealth for private gain.

Yet despite the UK’s similar decline in geopolitical relevance, living conditions and an education system in crisis, our students have not been rioting.

This could be on the horizon—progressive organisations have called for a youth strike on the 20 November—but why are we taking so long to catch up?

One aspect at play could be the different relationship to schools and schooling.

author: Freedom Editor
title: Buying politicians in the Land of the Free
content:
Radical Reprint: We head back eighteen years to another US political contest where money put paid to the idea of ‘free and fair’ elections

It’s election season in the US again this month, with midterm House and Senate contests likely to see a strong backlash against Donald Trump’s MAGA cult. Elections in the US are never free and fair—for one thing, they’re enormously expensive—but the overt threats from the current administration against election officials seem reminiscent of events at the denouement of Trump’s previous term in November 2020 to January 2021..

Nonetheless, the ubiquity of money in politics in the Land of the Free is a constant. Eighteen years ago in the presidential election that brought Barack Obama into office, our friend Louis Further covered the extent to which rich donors sought to evade campaign finance rules with great success. Since then, times have changed for the worse. The infamous Citizens United Supreme Court decision of 2010 treated corporations as people, and struck down limits on what corporations could spend in elections (ironically overturning a law on campaign finance restrictions sponsored by Obama’s 2008 rival John McCain).

Since then the only way has been up in terms of what corporations can and do spend to make sure they get as little scrutiny as possible, or that suitable candidates can be elected who can be expected to shamelessly do
